studies.title: Paid blue checks stopped working: 8 million days of X data show bought verification backfires
studies.paper_title: The impact of platform verification badges on social media influencer engagement
studies.the_study: Researchers combined influencer interviews, Reddit discussions, a controlled experiment and an analysis of more than 8 million daily observations from X to test how verification badges affect engagement under three regimes: merit-based, hybrid and fully purchasable. Verification consistently raised perceived authenticity, and authenticity drove perceived influence, which drove engagement. But once badges became buyable, the link from authenticity to perceived influence weakened and, under fully paid verification, reversed — so the badge stopped boosting engagement.
studies.why_it_matters: Platform trust signals are only worth what they cost to obtain; when a credential becomes a purchase, it can actively undercut the credibility marketers are paying for when they vet creators.
studies.story_angle_primary: If your influencer vetting checklist still treats a verification badge as a quality filter, this evidence suggests it may be noise or worse on platforms where checks are sold. Worth testing whether audience engagement on your own paid-creator campaigns tracks badges at all, and building alternative credibility signals — audience comments, longevity, third-party audits — into selection criteria.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The blue check used to mean someone vetted you; now it often means someone paid a subscription. The data suggests ordinary users have partly caught on, rewarding checked accounts less than they used to — a live case study in how quickly a trust symbol can be devalued.
studies.caveats: Primarily one platform (X) in a specific period of policy change; experimental component supplements but does not replace causal identification in the observational data; Reddit discussions are a self-selected, vocal sample.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, data scale and mediation chain all match the abstract; the digest slightly hardens "weakening its effect on engagement" into the badge no longer working at all.

studies.title: When Universal pulled its catalog from TikTok, Spotify streams fell — but only for the hits
studies.paper_title: Does TikTok promote or cannibalize music streaming? Estimands and identification with heavy-tailed outcomes
studies.the_study: Economists used Universal Music Group's global withdrawal of its catalog from TikTok as a quasi-natural experiment to estimate whether TikTok promotes or cannibalizes paid streaming, and showed that earlier contradictory findings stem largely from different difference-in-differences specifications weighting different parts of a highly skewed distribution. In their data the top 10% of songs account for 96% of TikTok creations and 76% of Spotify streams. Losing TikTok access reduced aggregate Spotify demand for UMG titles, with losses concentrated in viral songs and almost no meaningful change in the long tail; the 2025 US TikTok outage pointed the same way. Lost TikTok exposure also cut playlist inclusion, compounding the shock over time.
studies.why_it_matters: It settles a high-stakes industry argument with real market data: short-form video exposure is a genuine demand driver, but the value is overwhelmingly concentrated in a handful of breakout titles rather than spread across the catalog.
studies.story_angle_primary: For anyone negotiating platform licensing or budgeting social spend, the lesson is that averages lie when outcomes are heavy-tailed — the ROI question is not 'does this channel lift the typical SKU' but 'does it lift the few items that carry the P&L.' Also note the compounding mechanism: social exposure feeds algorithmic placement (playlists), so pulling back has a delayed second hit.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The songs you hear everywhere on TikTok are the same tiny fraction of tracks generating most streaming revenue — and when they vanish from the app, they lose ground on Spotify too. Discovery on one platform quietly determines what you get served on another.
studies.caveats: Observational quasi-experiment rather than a randomized test; music streaming only; findings depend on modeling choices the authors themselves show are consequential; focused on one label's catalog withdrawal plus one outage event.
studies.verdict_notes: Figures (top 10% = 96% of creations, 76% of streams), direction of effect, outage evidence and playlist mechanism all match; "settles" overstates a paper whose own point is that conclusions hinge on estimand choice.

studies.title: Meta-analysis of 97 studies: looks drive engagement, expertise drives purchase
studies.paper_title: When Social Media Influencers Work: A Meta‐Analysis of Brand Engagement, Behavioral Intention, and Boundary Conditions
studies.the_study: Researchers pooled 97 studies covering 40,330 participants and used meta-analytic structural equation modeling to separate the effects of influencer attractiveness, expertise and trustworthiness on brand engagement versus behavioral intention. Attractiveness was the only credibility attribute with a significant direct effect on brand engagement, while expertise had the strongest direct effect on behavioral intention, with trustworthiness and attractiveness also contributing. Brand engagement predicted behavioral intention, but the indirect paths from credibility through engagement were not significant, and cultural, economic and parasocial moderators showed little path-specific moderation.
studies.why_it_matters: It gives brands a casting rule of thumb: pick attractive creators when the objective is engagement metrics, pick credentialed experts when the objective is conversion — and stop assuming engagement is the bridge between the two.
studies.story_angle_primary: Test whether your influencer selection matches your actual KPI. The finding that engagement does not mediate credibility's effect on intention challenges the common practice of using likes and comments as a proxy for sales impact; a dual-roster approach (awareness creators vs. expert creators) is worth a controlled trial.
studies.story_angle_secondary: What makes you double-tap and what makes you buy are different things. Attractive creators win attention; people who visibly know the category are the ones who actually shift decisions — useful to notice in yourself the next time a recommendation lands.
studies.caveats: Synthesizes existing studies, most of which rely on self-reported intentions and surveys rather than observed purchases, so the underlying evidence base inherits those limits; moderator tests may be underpowered.
studies.verdict_notes: 97 studies, 40,330 participants, OSMASEM, the attractiveness/expertise split, the non-significant indirect paths and limited moderation are all faithfully reported; only the "contextual" moderator category is omitted from the list.

studies.title: What keeps creators loyal to a brand: autonomy, shared values, and being allowed to use AI
studies.paper_title: Building sustainable influencer partnerships within the creator economy
studies.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
studies.the_study: A two-phase mixed-methods study interviewed 22 professional influencers across four regions and then surveyed 422 influencers, testing with structural equation modeling how brand practices relate to partnership longevity. Brands that supported creative autonomy, aligned on ethical purpose and enabled AI co-creation were associated with higher influencer feelings of ownership over the collaboration and greater 'thriving,' which in turn linked to voluntary advocacy and intentions to continue the partnership.
studies.why_it_matters: As influencer deals shift from one-off posts to ongoing partnerships, the factors that retain creators look less like fees and more like the conditions that retain employees.
studies.story_angle_primary: If creator churn is eroding your campaign continuity, the levers tested here — loosening creative control, being explicit about brand purpose, and permitting rather than prohibiting AI tools in content production — are cheap to pilot against a control group of standard contracts. Treat it as a hypothesis to test in your own roster, not a proven retention formula.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The creators whose sponsored posts feel least scripted may be the ones whose brand partners gave them the most rope — a tell for audiences trying to judge whether an endorsement is genuine.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey of self-reported intentions, so causal direction cannot be established; sample is influencers themselves, not consumers or actual partnership outcomes; regions not specified in detail.
studies.verdict_notes: 22 interviews across four regions, 422 surveyed influencers, SEM and the ownership/thriving to advocacy and continuity pathways all match; associational language is used appropriately and limitations are flagged.

studies.title: B2B trust can now be built entirely online — at least on WeChat
studies.paper_title: Mechanisms for trust development in B2B relationships on social media
studies.the_study: A qualitative multiple-case study of seven B2B firms in China drew on 31 semi-structured interviews, netnography and documentary data to identify how interorganizational trust forms on social media. The authors identify five mechanisms — trusted content, partner endorsements, acquaintance-based guanxi, high customer stickiness, and interpersonal salesperson–customer trust — and argue that trust developed through individuals' personal use of culturally embedded platforms transfers to business relationships.
studies.why_it_matters: It challenges the long-held assumption in B2B selling that serious relationships must move offline, suggesting social platforms can carry a deal from first contact to trust.
studies.story_angle_primary: For B2B marketers, the actionable piece is 'platform trust transfer': trust people build using a platform personally spills into business dealings conducted there. Worth auditing whether your sales team is present on the platforms where buyers already live socially, and whether individual salespeople — not just the corporate account — are visible.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Limited direct relevance for consumers, beyond showing how blurred the line has become between personal messaging apps and professional dealmaking.
studies.caveats: Qualitative, seven firms, single country; Chinese platform ecosystem and guanxi norms may not generalize to LinkedIn-centric Western B2B; no quantitative test of outcomes.
studies.verdict_notes: Seven firms, 31 interviews, netnography, documentary data and the five mechanisms match exactly; the headline names a platform the abstract never mentions.

studies.title: The hidden variable in influencer campaigns: how much the pictures look alike
studies.paper_title: Visual strategies in influencer marketing campaigns: The role of consistency
studies.journal: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 707 posts and 1,105 Instagram stories from 182 influencer marketing campaigns, extracting 47 visual and consistency features across four dimensions: color, complexity, composition and content. Posts performed better when visually consistent across a campaign, while stories did best with a feature-specific mix of consistency and variation. The pattern depended on who was posting and what was sold: consistency paid off most for posts by macro influencers, whereas variation was positively linked to performance in stories by micro influencers, and product campaigns favored consistent posts but varied stories. Simulations showed a model-informed visual briefing beat both a 'no consistency rule' approach and a blanket 'be consistent' approach.
studies.why_it_matters: Brands typically brief influencers on messaging and hashtags but leave the visual look to the creator; this suggests campaign-level visual coherence is itself a performance lever, and that the right amount of it differs by format and influencer tier.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit your last three influencer campaigns for visual consistency in color, composition and complexity, then test a tiered brief: tighter visual guardrails for macro-influencer feed posts, looser ones for micro-influencer stories. Because this is observational campaign data rather than a randomized test, treat the simulated gains as a hypothesis to A/B test in your own next campaign.
studies.story_angle_secondary: That feeling that an influencer's sponsored posts all start looking the same is not accidental — visual sameness across a campaign is quietly associated with better engagement, which explains why your feed increasingly resembles a coordinated color story.
studies.caveats: Observational analysis of existing campaigns, so associations may reflect selection by brands and creators rather than causal effects; single platform (Instagram); performance gains from the 'model-informed strategy' come from simulation, not a live test.
studies.verdict_notes: Post/story/campaign counts, 47 features, four visual dimensions, the macro-post vs. micro-story pattern, product-campaign result and simulation framing all match; the abstract's mixed service-campaign findings are omitted but nothing is misstated.

studies.title: Some people are just wired to bond with influencers — and virtual ones can't cash in
studies.paper_title: The role of trait-based parasocial tendency in influencer marketing
studies.the_study: Across two controlled experiments (Study 1 pooled four data sets, N=1,385; Study 2, N=322), participants viewed identical ads featuring an unfamiliar human or virtual influencer and completed measures of dispositional 'parasocial tendency,' trust and purchase intention. People with a stronger general tendency to form one-sided bonds with media figures reported higher purchase intent, partly via trust — but that indirect path was significantly weaker for virtual influencers. In Study 2, parasocial tendency predicted trust in an endorsement only when the influencer was human and perceived as highly humanlike; for virtual influencers, high anthropomorphism actually canceled the effect.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the payoff from CGI and AI influencers is not evenly distributed: the very consumers most primed to bond with creators are the ones who discount virtual ones, and making a virtual influencer more humanlike may backfire rather than help.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are piloting a virtual or AI influencer, segment results by audience propensity to form creator attachments rather than reading average lift — and test whether leaning into realistic human likeness helps or triggers skepticism. These were controlled exposures to unfamiliar influencers, so the finding speaks to first impressions, not long-running character brands with established fandoms.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Whether you find an influencer trustworthy may say as much about your own personality as about them — and the more convincingly human a computer-generated creator looks, the more some viewers pull back.
studies.caveats: Experimental exposure to unfamiliar influencers rather than real, established relationships; outcomes are stated purchase intentions, not purchases; pooled data sets in Study 1 limit design transparency; no information on sample source or country in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Both study Ns, the pooled design, the weaker indirect path for virtual influencers and the anthropomorphism boundary condition are all accurate; "backfire" overstates a nullified effect.

studies.title: Personalized ads make people like you — and talk about you badly anyway
studies.paper_title: The personalization–privacy paradox in social media advertising: a cross-national study of ad attitudes and eWOM
studies.the_study: An online survey of Instagram users in three EU countries under the same GDPR regime but with differing privacy cultures (Poland N=337, Portugal N=200, Sweden N=196) measured perceived ad personalization, intrusiveness, ad attitudes and intentions to spread positive or negative word of mouth, analyzed with multi-group structural equation modeling. Personalization raised positive attitudes toward ads and intrusiveness lowered them, as expected. The twist: strong ad attitudes predicted higher intentions for negative electronic word of mouth as well as positive — an ambivalent response. Intrusiveness blunted the benefit of personalization in Portugal and Sweden but not in Poland.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests measuring 'ad liking' alone can mask a simultaneous willingness to complain about targeting, and that a single pan-European targeting setting may land differently market by market even under identical regulation.
studies.story_angle_primary: Track positive and negative word of mouth as separate outcomes in social ad testing rather than netting them into one sentiment score, and consider country-level calibration of targeting intensity within the EU rather than one GDPR-compliant default. This is self-reported attitude data, so treat it as a signal about where to look in your own campaign metrics.
studies.story_angle_secondary: People can enjoy an ad that clearly knows them and still feel uneasy enough to warn friends about it — the discomfort with targeting does not vanish just because the targeting is good.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey; cannot establish causation; measures intentions to share word of mouth rather than observed sharing; three countries and one platform (Instagram); Portuguese and Swedish samples just under 200.
studies.verdict_notes: Country samples (337/200/196), MGSEM, the ambivalent negative-eWOM finding and the Poland moderation exception are all correct; the headline and body use causal verbs for cross-sectional survey data, though the caveat notes the limit.

studies.title: In influencer persuasion, the voice may matter more than the face
studies.paper_title: Understanding influencer persuasion: facial and vocal pleasantness, social presence and dual involvement processes
studies.the_study: Researchers surveyed 626 followers of social media influencers about perceived facial pleasantness, vocal pleasantness and social presence, then modeled how these fed into narrative transportation, parasocial relationships, word of mouth and purchase intentions using structural equation modeling. Vocal pleasantness and perceived social presence were significantly associated with both getting absorbed in the influencer's story and forming a parasocial bond; facial pleasantness was not. Those two involvement processes were in turn linked to brand word of mouth and purchase intent.
studies.why_it_matters: Influencer selection and briefing heavily weight visual appeal and aesthetics, but this points to audio delivery and a sense of being spoken to directly as the underrated drivers of persuasion.
studies.story_angle_primary: Add vocal delivery and on-camera 'presence' to influencer casting criteria and creative briefs — test voiceover-led or direct-address formats against purely aesthetic, visually polished executions. The evidence is correlational self-report, so use it to justify an experiment, not to overhaul casting.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If you have ever wondered why one creator's recommendation feels like advice from a friend while a better-looking one's feels like an ad, the answer may be in how they sound and how directly they address you.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional survey of a single follower sample; cannot establish causation; all constructs including the 'nonverbal' cues are self-reported perceptions rather than objectively coded audio or video features; outcomes are stated intentions; country and recruitment source unspecified in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: 626 followers, SEM, the vocal-pleasantness and social-presence findings versus the null for facial pleasantness, and the downstream eWOM/purchase intention links all match; associational language and caveats are appropriate.

studies.title: For luxury brands, a smaller influencer may protect the aura of exclusivity
studies.paper_title: How Influencer Follower-Scale Popularity Erodes Luxury Brand Exclusivity: The Crowd Dilutes the Crown: How Micro-Influencers Reduce Social Crowding and Preserve Exclusivity
studies.the_study: Across five studies — four experiments plus a field test — researchers compared consumer responses to luxury brand posts from macro-influencers (very large follower counts) versus micro-influencers. Micro-influencers produced higher purchase and brand usage intentions, and the effect ran through two linked mechanisms: they reduced the sense that 'everyone' already has the product (perceived social crowding) and strengthened perceived brand exclusivity. The exclusivity route was strongest among consumers high in Consumer Need for Uniqueness, and both routes weakened among consumers experiencing luxury fatigue.
studies.why_it_matters: Influencer-tier selection is usually treated as a reach-versus-cost decision; this suggests that for luxury, follower count is itself a signal that can work against the brand by implying mass adoption.
studies.story_angle_primary: Worth testing in your own campaigns: split-test micro versus macro creators on exclusivity-sensitive lines and measure perceived crowding, not just reach and engagement. The field test component makes this stronger than a pure lab result, but tier effects may differ by category, price point and market.
studies.story_angle_secondary: A quiet lesson in how desire works: seeing a bag on a mega-influencer's feed can make it feel less special, not more. Your sense that a brand is 'over' often comes from how many people you see with it rather than anything about the product.
studies.caveats: Experimental studies likely used online panels with intention measures; the field test is described only briefly, with limited detail on setting and scale. Findings are specific to luxury categories where exclusivity is central.
studies.verdict_notes: Five studies (four experiments plus a field test), the dual crowding/exclusivity mechanism, the CNFU boundary condition and the luxury-fatigue attenuation are all reported correctly, with both moderators retained.

studies.title: When a customer swears at your brand online, a gracious reply wins fewer bystanders
studies.paper_title: Mind your tone: how swear words in online complaints influence bystander perceptions of airlines and hotels
studies.journal: Journal of Service Theory and Practice
studies.the_study: Two scenario experiments with US consumers — one set in the airline industry (N=679), one in hotels (N=553) — showed people a public social media complaint and a brand response, varying whether the complaint was civil or uncivil (containing swear words) and whether the brand's reply was accommodative. Accommodative responses raised bystanders' purchase intentions, fully mediated by brand attitude. But the payoff was significantly weaker when the original complaint was profane: bystanders appear to judge the brand's reply partly through the lens of the customer's tone.
studies.why_it_matters: Service teams are typically trained to respond accommodatively to every public complaint; this indicates the reputational return on that effort varies sharply with how the complainant behaved.
studies.story_angle_primary: Consider tone-sensitive response playbooks: the generous public apology may earn most of its goodwill on civil complaints, while abusive threads may warrant a short reply and a move to private channels. Test whether de-escalating or redirecting hostile threads protects brand attitude better than full accommodation in the feed.
studies.story_angle_secondary: If you want a company to look bad — or want other customers to take your side — swearing may backfire. Onlookers read the whole exchange, and an uncivil complaint appears to blunt the credit a brand earns for responding well, muddying the signal for everyone watching.
studies.caveats: Hypothetical scenarios with stated purchase intentions rather than real complaint threads or purchases; online US samples; two service categories only; single country.
studies.verdict_notes: Design, samples and main moderated-mediation finding match the abstract; the consumer-facing angle reverses the practical implication and attributes to the study an outcome (judgments of the complainer) it did not measure.

studies.title: Sponsorship labels hurt 'here are the specs' influencer posts more than stories
studies.paper_title: The persuasive power of social media influencers: the effects of product congruence, altruistic motivation and storytelling
studies.the_study: Three studies with Chinese social media users recruited via the Credamo platform (total N=735) tested how influencer–product fit drives purchase intention. A survey established that congruence works partly by making the endorsement feel altruistically motivated — as if the influencer genuinely wants to help. Two follow-up experiments (2x2 and 2x2x2 designs) found storytelling posts amplified the congruence effect, while informational posts lost persuasive power once a sponsorship disclosure was attached.
studies.why_it_matters: Disclosure is mandatory in most markets, so the practical question is which creative formats survive it — and narrative content appears more resilient than straight product information.
studies.story_angle_primary: If paid partnerships must be labeled, test shifting briefs toward first-person narrative rather than feature lists, and check whether tightly fitted creator–product matches maintain the 'she really uses this' read once the ad label appears. Sample sizes per cell are modest, so treat this as a hypothesis to validate on your own campaigns.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Your skepticism is format-dependent: an '#ad' tag makes a spec-heavy review feel like a commercial, but a personal story tends to slip past the same defenses. Knowing that may help you notice when you are being sold to.
studies.caveats: All three studies used a Chinese online panel with hypothetical posts and stated purchase intentions; single country; study 1 is cross-sectional and cannot establish causation.
studies.verdict_notes: Design (three studies, Credamo panel in China, N=735), the altruistic-motivation mediator, and the post-type and disclosure moderators all match the abstract; caveats are appropriate.

studies.title: Telling people an environmental image was AI-generated drains the guilt out of it
studies.paper_title: Influence of environmental stimuli on sustainable food choices: the moderating role of AI-source disclosure
studies.the_study: Three studies examined how positive nature imagery versus negative environmental-damage imagery affects food choices. Both types of stimuli reduced choices of meat-heavy meals relative to a control. The mechanisms differed: positive imagery worked through feeling connected to nature, negative imagery through guilt, with both routing into greater consideration of future consequences. In study 3, disclosing that the imagery was AI-generated significantly weakened the guilt response to negative stimuli, while leaving the nature-connectedness response to positive stimuli intact.
studies.why_it_matters: As brands and public health campaigns lean on generative imagery, this suggests AI disclosure selectively undercuts fear- and guilt-based appeals while sparing warmer, aspirational ones.
studies.story_angle_primary: If you are using AI-generated visuals in sustainability, health or cause communications, consider testing disclosure effects by appeal type — guilt-driven creative may be the most fragile once audiences know a machine made the picture. Aspirational nature imagery looks more robust.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Guilt seems to require a believable victim. Learning that a shocking environmental image was synthetic appears to let people off the emotional hook, even though the underlying facts have not changed — a useful thing to notice about your own reactions to online imagery.
studies.caveats: Choice tasks in study settings rather than real meal purchases; the AI-disclosure interaction on actual meat choice was not significant (the effect appeared on the guilt pathway); details of sample sourcing and size are limited in the abstract.
studies.verdict_notes: Three studies, the two mediation pathways and the AI-disclosure moderation are all reported correctly, and the caveat correctly flags that the disclosure x stimuli interaction on meat-heavy choice was not significant.

studies.title: Let the robot be casual and the human be formal: mismatched tone earns more forgiveness after a service failure
studies.paper_title: The interactive influence of service recovery agent and language style on consumer forgiveness: mediation of perceived sincerity
studies.journal: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
studies.the_study: Four scenario experiments across hotel, restaurant and e-commerce contexts, with 866 participants recruited online, crossed the recovery agent (human vs. robot) with language style (formal vs. informal). Consumers forgave most when robots apologized informally and humans apologized formally — a complementary rather than congruent fit — with perceived sincerity as the mediator. The robot-informal advantage was stronger for minor failures and less loyal customers; the human-formal advantage was stronger for severe failures and highly loyal customers.
studies.why_it_matters: Companies rolling out chatbots and service bots often script them to sound as human and chummy as possible while pushing human agents toward casual tone too; this indicates the optimal pairing may run the other way.
studies.story_angle_primary: Audit the tone scripts for automated service recovery separately from human ones, and test a casual voice for bots on low-severity issues while keeping human agents formal on serious failures and with your best customers. These are scenario experiments, so validate on live tickets before rewriting the playbook.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Why a breezy 'Oops, our bad!' from a company can feel insulting when something really went wrong — and oddly fine coming from a chatbot over a late delivery. Sincerity is read from the fit between who is speaking and how.
studies.caveats: Hypothetical scenarios and stated forgiveness rather than observed behavior; online sample; likely single-country (Asia-Pacific journal context); no real service interactions.
studies.verdict_notes: Four scenario experiments, N=866 recruited online, complementary-fit result, perceived sincerity mediator, and both boundary conditions (failure severity, loyalty) match the abstract.

studies.title: Inside China's livestream selling machine: what the hosts and their agencies say actually drives sales
studies.paper_title: Campaign success and activity-system contradictions in livestream influencer marketing
studies.the_study: A rare supply-side study of livestream influencer marketing drew on 65 in-depth interviews, primarily with livestream influencers and staff at multi-channel networks (the agencies that manage them), plus brand sponsors, platform representatives and viewers, alongside surveys of 112 influencers and 100 agency team members working on China's four leading livestream platforms. Data were collected in two waves (2021 and 2024). Participants identified influencer capability, influencer–agency coordination and platform strategy as the dominant success factors, and the study documents the tensions between hosts and agencies — over tools, targets and platform policy — and the workarounds both sides develop.
studies.why_it_matters: Brands buying livestream slots typically see only the host; this maps the team, incentives and platform rules behind the screen that determine whether a campaign converts.
studies.story_angle_primary: Use it as a due-diligence checklist for livestream partnerships: ask about the agency's coordination model and platform relationships, not just the host's follower count, and watch how policy changes on a platform reshape what a campaign can deliver. The 2021-to-2024 comparison also shows how fast the operating environment shifts.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The chatty host selling you a lipstick at midnight is the front end of a production team with sales quotas and platform algorithms to manage — context that makes the urgency and scarcity cues on screen easier to read.
studies.caveats: Qualitative and descriptive rather than causal; success factors are participants' perceptions, not measured campaign outcomes; confined to China's four leading platforms; modest survey samples (112 and 100).
studies.verdict_notes: Interview and survey counts, two-wave design and success factors are reported accurately; two small wording stretches ('dominant' factors; 'targets' as a source of tension).

studies.title: The harsh reviewer problem: negativity reads as helpful but makes the critic look less trustworthy
studies.paper_title: Are Critics More Credible? When Positivity Is Expected, Negative Reviewers Are Perceived to Be Less Credible
studies.the_study: Across 19 studies with 7,330 participants spanning multiple product categories, researchers tested how the valence of a review shapes perceptions of the reviewer. Negative reviewers were consistently rated as less credible than positive ones, even though their reviews were judged more helpful — the driver being an expectancy violation, since people assume reviews will skew positive. The penalty disappeared when expectations were ambiguous and flipped entirely when people expected negativity, and it carried downstream costs: less willingness to follow the reviewer's next recommendation or to follow them on social media.
studies.why_it_matters: It complicates the standard assumption that critical voices are the most trusted ones, and suggests that a creator's credibility depends less on honesty than on whether their tone matches what the audience expected going in.
studies.story_angle_primary: For brands managing influencer rosters or review ecosystems, this hints that the context an audience brings matters as much as the content: in categories where glowing reviews are the norm, a critical take may damage the critic more than the brand. Worth testing whether seeding realistic expectations — or partnering with creators known for a critical stance — changes how negative coverage lands.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Consumers may be systematically discounting exactly the reviews that would help them most. If you find yourself dismissing a scathing one-star review as someone with an axe to grind, the research suggests that reaction is often about broken social norms rather than the reviewer's actual reliability.
studies.caveats: Experimental studies using reviewer profiles and scenarios rather than observed purchase or following behavior; credibility and willingness-to-follow are measured judgments, not platform data.
studies.verdict_notes: 19 studies, N=7,330, the expectancy-violation mechanism and downstream follow/recommendation effects are all accurate; one boundary condition is stated more strongly than the abstract supports.

studies.title: When your doctor is also an influencer, your skepticism switches off
studies.paper_title: When Doctors Become Influencers: How Social Media Presence Disarms Persuasion Knowledge and Shapes Consumer Behaviors
studies.the_study: A mixed-methods project across two studies analyzed how physicians present themselves on social media and how consumers respond to them. The researchers found that doctor-influencers lean heavily on competence signaling while adding carefully selected personal touches, a combination that preserves authority while muting the sense that they are selling something. The authors propose a "mere social media presence effect": simply having a visible social platform appears to disarm consumers' persuasion knowledge and boost perceived effectiveness beyond a traditional expert-to-patient interaction.
studies.why_it_matters: Credentialed professionals are becoming a distinct and unusually persuasive class of influencer, and the same mechanism that improves adherence to genuine medical advice also lowers consumers' guard against commercial recommendations.
studies.story_angle_primary: Health, wellness and supplement brands are already courting credentialed creators; the finding suggests the persuasive lift comes partly from audiences not registering the content as marketing at all. That raises a disclosure and reputational risk worth getting ahead of rather than exploiting.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The white-coat effect survives the jump to TikTok and Instagram. Knowing that a doctor's follower-friendly mix of expertise plus a glimpse of personal life is a deliberate self-presentation strategy is a useful prompt to ask who is paying for the post.
studies.caveats: Qualitative and mixed-methods design with a theory-building emphasis rather than large-scale behavioral evidence; sample sizes and country not specified in the abstract; recommendation adherence is proposed rather than directly observed.
studies.verdict_notes: Body text correctly presents the 'mere social media presence effect' as proposed, but the headline and 'Why it matters' state a theory-building mechanism as an established effect and extend it to commercial endorsements the abstract does not cover.

studies.title: Fast-moving brands on social media earn more word of mouth — but mainly from collectivist consumers
studies.paper_title: Cultural echoes in e-WOM: the role of self-presentation in brand agility perception
studies.the_study: Three online experiments tested whether consumers' perception that a brand is agile on social media — quick, responsive, adaptive — drives positive electronic word of mouth. Studies 1 and 2 compared adult samples in Türkiye and the UK; Study 3 replicated the model within the UK alone using an individual-level measure of collectivism. Perceived social media agility raised e-WOM intentions everywhere, but the effect was substantially stronger among Turkish participants, and within the UK it only really kicked in once a person's individual collectivism score passed a threshold.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests the payoff from staffing a rapid-response social team is not uniform across markets, and that within any single market it concentrates among a subset of consumers with more communal orientations.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before globalizing an always-on social response playbook, brands could test whether agility actually converts into sharing and advocacy in each market — the returns may be far larger in collectivist-leaning audiences than in individualistic ones, where self-presentation motives complicate the picture.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Why some people rush to praise a brand that replied fast while others shrug: the research points to cultural orientation, and to whether posting about the brand says something flattering about you.
studies.caveats: Online adult panels with hypothetical brand scenarios and stated e-WOM intentions rather than observed sharing; nationality used as a proxy for culture in two of three studies; only two countries compared.
studies.verdict_notes: Three-study design, the Türkiye/UK comparison and the Johnson-Neyman collectivism threshold are reported correctly; the self-presentation moderator is missing from the study description and one effect-size word is firmer than the abstract.

studies.title: Creepy targeting doesn't just annoy people — it makes them want to blend into the crowd
studies.paper_title: The Conformity Effects of Personalized Advertising: When Consumers Seek Social Anonymity
studies.the_study: Across seven experiments, researchers tested what personalized social media advertising does to consumers beyond the familiar privacy backlash. They found that ads visibly built on personal data raise privacy concern, which heightens a desire for social anonymity — and that desire in turn pushes people toward conformity, choosing the popular or majority option rather than standing out. The effect was shaped by consumers' perceived self-control capacity, and the researchers also tested surveillance cues as a design lever marketers could use.
studies.why_it_matters: If being tracked nudges people to hide in the crowd, personalization may be quietly reshaping which products get chosen — favoring bestsellers and mainstream options over distinctive or niche ones.
studies.story_angle_primary: Worth testing whether your personalized placements shift the mix of what people buy, not just click-through: if targeted environments tilt shoppers toward safe, popular choices, brands built on distinctiveness may be disadvantaged by the very channels they pay most for. Treat this as a hypothesis to validate in your own data rather than an established effect.
studies.story_angle_secondary: That uneasy feeling when an ad knows too much may change more than your mood — it can make you want to disappear into the majority, and the safest-looking option suddenly looks more appealing.
studies.caveats: Seven lab/online experiments rather than field data; abstract does not specify samples, countries or whether purchases were real or hypothetical.
studies.verdict_notes: Seven experiments, the privacy concern to social anonymity to conformity chain, the self-control moderator and the surveillance-cue element all match; the extrapolation about bestsellers is appropriately hedged and caveated.

studies.title: "The AI did it" is a risky excuse: blaming the algorithm cuts blame but signals moral indifference
studies.paper_title: Exemption or backfire? The double-edged effect of AI attribution strategy on brand trust in digital content moral crises
studies.journal: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
studies.the_study: Using five scenario-based experiments, researchers examined how consumers react when a brand blames an AI system for content that violates widely shared social values. Attributing the failure to AI did reduce perceived responsibility — an exemption effect that helped repair trust — but it simultaneously raised perceptions of moral indifference, which damaged trust. Which path dominated depended on context: widely dispersed negative word of mouth strengthened the exemption path, while low dispersion strengthened the backfire; consumers with higher AI literacy were more forgiving, while those prone to hostile attribution bias were more suspicious of the brand's technical explanation.
studies.why_it_matters: As AI-generated brand content scales, "it was an AI error" is becoming a default crisis line — and this evidence suggests it can simultaneously reduce blame and make a brand look like it doesn't care.
studies.story_angle_primary: Pressure-test your crisis playbook: pairing an AI explanation with an explicit statement of ownership and values may be necessary to neutralize the moral-indifference read. These are scenario experiments, so treat the two-sided effect as a warning to stress-test messaging, not a finished script.
studies.story_angle_secondary: When a company says a machine made the offensive post, notice your own reaction — research suggests most people accept that the brand is less factually to blame while trusting it less as a moral actor.
studies.caveats: Scenario-based experiments with hypothetical brands and crises rather than real incidents; abstract does not report sample sizes, countries or panel sources; stated trust rather than observed behavior.
studies.verdict_notes: Five scenario experiments, the double-edged exemption/backfire effect, the eWOM-dispersion moderator and both consumer traits are reported accurately; one consumer-facing line converts an average effect into a claim about 'most people'.

studies.title: ASMR ads land very differently for "masculine" and "feminine" brands — 15,807 YouTube comments show why
studies.paper_title: Whisper Sounds Become Mindful Relaxation: A Computational Analysis of Consumer Responses to ASMR Advertising
studies.the_study: Researchers text-mined 15,807 YouTube comments on ASMR advertising to see how audiences actually talk about whisper-and-trigger-sound marketing. Six themes emerged: sexualized whisper cues, mindful relaxation, purchase discussion, hand-sound triggers, sleep-related immersion, and audience reactions. Brands with a feminine brand personality drew higher immersion scores, while masculine brands drew more sexualization-oriented discourse.
studies.why_it_matters: ASMR is a cheap, high-engagement sensory format, but this suggests the same technique can be read as calming relaxation or as sexualized content depending on the brand's existing gender coding — a brand-safety and positioning risk hiding inside a trend.
studies.story_angle_primary: Before commissioning ASMR creative, audit how your brand's gendered personality is likely to frame it, and monitor comment sections as a live read on whether audiences are landing on "relaxing" or "suggestive." This is observational comment data, so it shows how conversation skews, not what it does to sales.
studies.story_angle_secondary: The whisper videos in your feed aren't interpreted the same way by everyone — the brand attached to the sound shifts whether viewers experience it as mindfulness or as flirtation.
studies.caveats: Observational analysis of self-selected YouTube commenters on a single platform; comment discourse is not purchase behavior; no causal test; brand set and categories not specified.
studies.verdict_notes: Study facts (15,807 comments, six topics, gendered brand personality pattern) match the abstract; only the headline's "show why" and the verb "drew" nudge an associational text-mining result toward explanation.

studies.title: Crowdfunding titles that brag about market traction win; titles that get personal lose
studies.paper_title: Commercial or relational cues: how information salience in project titles affects crowdfunding performance
studies.the_study: Researchers analyzed 2,064 startup campaigns on the Chinese crowdfunding platform Kaishiba to see how the information made salient in a project title relates to funding outcomes. Titles foregrounding market validation — evidence that the product had traction or demand — were associated with better funding performance, while titles using low-psychological-distance, relational cues performed worse. Entrepreneur gender moderated the effect: projects did better when title cues matched gender stereotypes and worse when they cut against them.
studies.why_it_matters: Titles are a few words of free positioning, and this real-market data suggests commercial proof beats warmth — while also documenting a stereotype penalty founders pay for choosing the "wrong" framing.
studies.story_angle_primary: For anyone writing campaign, product or launch headlines, test validation-first phrasing against relational phrasing — and note the uncomfortable finding that backer responses to the same cue depend on who is asking, which is a bias worth measuring rather than accommodating.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Backers say they fund people, but the data from more than 2,000 campaigns suggests they respond to evidence of demand — and, less flatteringly, to whether the pitch matches gender expectations.
studies.caveats: Correlational analysis of one Chinese crowdfunding platform; no experimental manipulation, so causality is not established; findings may not generalize to Kickstarter-style Western platforms or categories.
studies.verdict_notes: Sample (2,064 startups, Kaishiba), direction of both title-cue effects and the gender-stereotype moderator all match; the platform's country is not stated in the abstract and the headline verbs run slightly ahead of correlational data (already caveated).

studies.title: Being outnumbered changes what people buy: gender-minority settings boost appeal of gender-neutral products
studies.paper_title: Affirming the self through products: how gender minority contexts drive appeal for gender-neutral products
studies.the_study: Three pre-registered experiments with respondents in the US, India, the UAE and Sweden tested how being in a numerical gender minority — for example, being one of few men or few women in a setting — affects reactions to deliberately gender-neutral products. People in gender-minority contexts rated gender-neutral products as more aligned with their own gender identity and reported higher purchase intentions, with self-verification mediating the effect. Cultural masculinity moderated how strongly minority status translated into purchase intention.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests gender-neutral products aren't only for consumers with fluid identities — the situation a shopper is in can make unisex offerings feel personally affirming even to people with traditional gender identification.
studies.story_angle_primary: Consider context, not just consumer segments, when placing gender-neutral lines: environments where your target is outnumbered may be the most receptive settings, and cultural differences mean the same product story won't travel unchanged across markets. Test in-market before scaling from these lab results.
studies.story_angle_secondary: Why a unisex product can suddenly feel right: when you're the odd one out in a room, choosing something that doesn't declare a gender can feel like a way of confirming who you are rather than erasing it.
studies.caveats: Pre-registered but lab/online experiments measuring purchase intentions rather than actual purchases; sample sizes and recruitment sources not specified in the abstract; four countries sampled across different studies rather than uniformly.
studies.verdict_notes: Design (three pre-registered experiments; US, India, UAE, Sweden across different studies), the self-verification mediator and the cultural-masculinity moderator are all reported accurately; the headline converts purchase intention into purchase.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** Across this batch, the cues audiences use to decide who to believe are all coming loose at once — and the labels meant to fix that are behaving unpredictably. Bought verification badges stopped lifting engagement and eventually reversed ("Paid blue checks stopped working," W7214149214); sponsorship disclosure gutted the persuasiveness of spec-style posts while narrative posts sailed through (W7212040284); telling people an image was AI-generated drained the guilt out of it (W7213456793); blaming an AI for a brand failure cut blame but read as moral indifference (W7214331895); negative reviewers were judged less credible precisely for being critical (W7172001493); doctor-influencers appear to switch off persuasion knowledge simply by having a feed (W7213976385); and virtual influencers lose exactly the consumers most inclined to bond with creators, with more humanlike CGI making it worse (W7213316341).

**Why pitch this now:** Paid verification is standard across X, Meta and LinkedIn, AI labeling rules are landing under the EU AI Act and platform provenance schemes, and disclosure enforcement by the FTC and ASA is tightening — all at the moment generative content is flooding feeds, so the entire apparatus of trust signaling is being rebuilt in public with almost no evidence that it works as intended.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the collapse and reconstruction of credibility signals online: what the evidence says each label actually does to audiences, why some disclosures suppress persuasion and others quietly license it, and what brands and platforms are left with when a badge can be bought and a photograph can be generated. Aimed at marketers, platform watchers and policy-literate general readers.

**Potential headlines:**
- Paid checkmarks, AI labels and #ad tags: the research on what disclosure actually does to audiences
- Tell people the picture was fake and the guilt disappears
- Every signal you use to decide who to trust online is now for sale or synthetic

**Potential outlets:**
- **Digiday** — covers creator vetting and platform trust economics closely, and the paid-verification and virtual-influencer findings speak directly to how agencies build rosters.
- **MIT Sloan Management Review** — suits the strategic framing of credibility as an asset firms can devalue by monetizing it, with the AI-blame crisis evidence as the hook for executives.
- **Wired** — the AI-disclosure results (guilt evaporating, "the AI did it" backfiring) fit its coverage of provenance labeling and synthetic media policy for a general technical readership.
- **The Atlantic** — a natural home for the broader cultural argument that verification and disclosure symbols are decaying faster than institutions can replace them, grounded in the review-credibility and doctor-influencer findings.

---
pitch_ideas_raw:
- **Paid blue checks stopped working (Work ID W7214149214):** Eight million days of X data showing bought badges stopped lifting engagement — and eventually hurt it — is a hard-numbers news story about a platform business model, for a marketing-trade news brief or a tech-business news desk.
- **When Universal pulled its catalog from TikTok (Work ID W4399061707):** A quasi-experiment that settles the "does TikTok cannibalize streaming?" fight and shows the value sits almost entirely in the top 10% of songs, for a music-business or media-economics feature.
- **Meta-analysis of 97 studies on influencer credibility (Work ID W7213954552):** Engagement does not mediate credibility's effect on intention, so likes are a poor proxy for sales — a direct challenge to standard influencer KPIs, for a CMO-audience column.
- **What keeps creators loyal to a brand (Work ID W7214020197):** Creator retention now looks like employee retention — autonomy, shared values and permission to use AI tools — for a creator-economy trade piece or an HR-flavored business column.
- **B2B trust built entirely online on WeChat (Work ID W7172485804):** "Platform trust transfer" as an argument that B2B deals no longer need to move offline, for a B2B marketing or sales-leadership trade explainer.
- **The hidden variable in influencer campaigns (Work ID W7172486915):** Visual consistency across a campaign is itself a performance lever, but the right dose differs by format and creator tier — a practical, testable briefing story for an advertising-craft or creative-strategy section.
- **Some people are just wired to bond with influencers (Work ID W7213316341):** Making a virtual influencer more humanlike can cancel its trust advantage with the very audiences most prone to parasocial bonds, for a marketing-trade news brief or an AI-in-advertising explainer.
- **Personalized ads make people like you — and talk about you badly anyway (Work ID W7214160679):** Positive and negative word of mouth rise together, so netting them into one sentiment score hides the problem; plus country-level divergence under identical GDPR rules, for a European marketing-trade analysis.
- **In influencer persuasion, the voice may matter more than the face (Work ID W7214151150):** Vocal pleasantness and social presence predicted absorption and parasocial bonding while facial attractiveness did not — a casting-criteria rethink, for a brand or creative-strategy column.
- **For luxury brands, a smaller influencer protects exclusivity (Work ID W7214325049):** Mega-influencer reach can signal mass adoption and reduce desire, with a field test behind it, for a luxury or retail trade feature.
- **When a customer swears at your brand online (Work ID W7214100498):** Bystanders give brands less credit for a gracious reply when the complaint was profane — an argument for tone-sensitive response playbooks, for a customer-service or PR trade piece.
- **Sponsorship labels hurt "here are the specs" posts more than stories (Work ID W7212040284):** Which creative formats survive mandatory disclosure, and why narrative slips past defenses that spec lists don't, for an influencer-marketing trade explainer or a consumer-psychology piece on ad literacy.
- **Telling people an environmental image was AI-generated drains the guilt (Work ID W7213456793):** AI disclosure selectively kills guilt-based appeals while sparing aspirational ones — a warning for sustainability and public-health campaigners, for a cause-marketing or science-communication outlet.
- **Let the robot be casual and the human be formal (Work ID W7213543402):** Complementary rather than matching tone earns forgiveness after service failures, contradicting how most chatbots are scripted, for a CX/service-design trade explainer.
- **Inside China's livestream selling machine (Work ID W7204239811):** A rare supply-side map of hosts, agencies and platform rules, with 2021-to-2024 change built in — a due-diligence read for brands buying livestream slots, for a retail or global-commerce trade feature.
- **The harsh reviewer problem (Work ID W7172001493):** Nineteen studies showing critical reviewers are seen as more helpful but less credible, because negativity violates expectations — a strong consumer-psychology explainer for a general-interest outlet or personal-finance/shopping column.
- **When your doctor is also an influencer (Work ID W7213976385):** The "mere social media presence effect" disarms persuasion knowledge, which is great for adherence and risky for supplements — for a health-business news piece or a consumer-affairs column.
- **Fast-moving brands earn more word of mouth — mainly from collectivist consumers (Work ID W7213466946):** The ROI of an always-on social response team may not survive the trip across markets, for an international-marketing trade analysis.
- **Creepy targeting makes people want to blend into the crowd (Work ID W7214349274):** If personalization nudges shoppers toward bestsellers, challenger and niche brands may be disadvantaged by the channels they pay most for — a genuinely new angle for a retail-trade or e-commerce strategy piece.
- **"The AI did it" is a risky excuse (Work ID W7214331895):** Blaming an algorithm cuts blame but signals moral indifference — a crisis-communications story with a clear playbook implication, for PR trade press.
- **ASMR ads land differently for "masculine" and "feminine" brands (Work ID W7214311277):** 15,807 comments show the same whisper ad reads as mindfulness or as sexualized content depending on brand gender coding — a brand-safety angle for an advertising trade outlet.
- **Crowdfunding titles that brag about traction win (Work ID W7213972386):** Validation cues beat warmth across 2,064 campaigns, with a documented penalty for founders whose framing cuts against gender stereotypes, for a startup/entrepreneurship outlet or a business-bias column.
- **Being outnumbered changes what people buy (Work ID W7214404629):** Gender-neutral products appeal most to people who are in a numerical gender minority in the moment — context beats segment, for a consumer-psychology explainer or a product-marketing trade piece.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: Marketing Research Digest — Social Media & Influencers — 2026-09-27
**Checked:** 2026-09-27 | **Studies reviewed:** 23
**Primary audience:** marketers and brand leaders | **Secondary audience:** general readers and consumers

---

### Study 1: Paid blue checks stopped working: 8 million days of X data show bought verification backfires
**Work ID:** W7214149214 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Effect overstated as elimination** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "under fully paid verification, reversed — so the badge stopped boosting engagement."
- **Abstract says:** "its effect on perceived influence is reduced and reversed under fully paid verification, weakening its effect on engagement."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports a weakened effect on engagement, not a complete loss of the engagement benefit; the reversal is specific to the authenticity-to-perceived-influence path.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "...reversed, weakening the badge's effect on engagement.""

**Issue B. Headline wording stronger than abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "8 million days of X data show bought verification backfires"
- **Abstract says:** "we found verification increases perceived authenticity, which in turn enhances perceived influence... its effect on perceived influence is reduced and reversed under fully paid verification, weakening its effect on engagement"
- **Problem:** "Backfires" implies net harm to engagement, whereas the abstract only reports a reversed intermediate path and a weakened engagement effect. Also, "8 million days" recasts "over 8 million daily observations" as a time span.
- **Suggested fix:** "Try "more than 8 million daily observations show bought verification loses its engagement payoff"."

### Study 2: When Universal pulled its catalog from TikTok, Spotify streams fell — but only for the hits
**Work ID:** W4399061707 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Settles the argument" overclaim** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "It settles a high-stakes industry argument with real market data"
- **Abstract says:** "Recent studies using this quasi-natural experiment have reached different conclusions... We show that these differences arise in part because the estimand changes with the specification."
- **Problem:** The paper's contribution is to explain why prior estimates diverge and to guide estimand choice, not to deliver a definitive settlement; the digest's own caveat about consequential modeling choices sits awkwardly with "settles".
- **Suggested fix:** "Rephrase as "It reconciles conflicting prior estimates and shows where the value is concentrated.""

### Study 3: Meta-analysis of 97 studies: looks drive engagement, expertise drives purchase
**Work ID:** W7213954552 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 4: What keeps creators loyal to a brand: autonomy, shared values, and being allowed to use AI
**Work ID:** W7214020197 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 5: B2B trust can now be built entirely online — at least on WeChat
**Work ID:** W7172485804 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Platform named but not in abstract** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "B2B trust can now be built entirely online — at least on WeChat"
- **Abstract says:** "a qualitative multiple-case study design involving seven B2B firms operating in China... trust developed through individuals' personal use of culturally embedded platforms transfers to and enhances B2B relationships"
- **Problem:** The abstract refers only to social media and "culturally embedded platforms" in China; WeChat is never specified. Unverifiable from abstract only, and readers may take it as a documented platform-specific result.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change the headline to "...at least on Chinese social platforms" or confirm the platform from the full text before naming it."

### Study 6: The hidden variable in influencer campaigns: how much the pictures look alike
**Work ID:** W7172486915 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 7: Some people are just wired to bond with influencers — and virtual ones can't cash in
**Work ID:** W7213316341 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Nullified effect described as backfiring** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "making a virtual influencer more humanlike may backfire rather than help"
- **Abstract says:** "For VIs, high anthropomorphism nullified the effect."
- **Problem:** Nullifying an effect is not the same as producing a negative one; "backfire" implies humanlike design actively reduces trust, which the abstract does not report.
- **Suggested fix:** "Say "making a virtual influencer more humanlike appears to cancel the benefit rather than add to it.""

### Study 8: Personalized ads make people like you — and talk about you badly anyway
**Work ID:** W7214160679 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Causal framing of survey data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Personalized ads make people like you — and talk about you badly anyway"
- **Abstract says:** "We conducted an online survey of Instagram users in three target countries... The results consistently indicate that higher personalization fosters more positive attitudes toward ads"
- **Problem:** A cross-sectional survey analyzed with SEM supports association, not causation; the headline asserts that personalized ads cause both liking and complaining.
- **Suggested fix:** "Rephrase as "Liking a personalized ad goes with wanting to complain about it" or add "linked to" phrasing."

**Issue B. Country characterization not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "three EU countries under the same GDPR regime but with differing privacy cultures"
- **Abstract says:** "comparing three EU countries (Poland, Portugal and Sweden) that operate under GDPR but differ in digital literacy and privacy concerns"
- **Problem:** "Privacy cultures" substitutes for the abstract's specific dimensions of digital literacy and privacy concerns; minor but changes the stated basis for comparison.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use "differing digital literacy and privacy concerns"."

### Study 9: In influencer persuasion, the voice may matter more than the face
**Work ID:** W7214151150 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 10: For luxury brands, a smaller influencer may protect the aura of exclusivity
**Work ID:** W7214325049 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 11: When a customer swears at your brand online, a gracious reply wins fewer bystanders
**Work ID:** W7214100498 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Consumer angle reverses the implication** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "If you want a company to look bad — or want other customers to take your side — swearing may backfire."
- **Abstract says:** "Complaint tone moderated this indirect effect such that the positive impact of accommodative responses was stronger for civil complaints and weaker for uncivil complaints."
- **Problem:** The study measured bystanders' brand attitude and purchase intentions, not how bystanders judge or side with the complainer. And on the measured outcome, an uncivil complaint reduces the goodwill the brand earns — which works in favor of, not against, a complainer who wants the company to look bad.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reframe as: 'An uncivil complaint blunts the credit a brand earns for responding well — though the study did not measure how bystanders judge the complainer themselves.'"

### Study 12: Sponsorship labels hurt 'here are the specs' influencer posts more than stories
**Work ID:** W7212040284 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 13: Telling people an environmental image was AI-generated drains the guilt out of it
**Work ID:** W7213456793 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 14: Let the robot be casual and the human be formal: mismatched tone earns more forgiveness after a service failure
**Work ID:** W7213543402 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 15: Inside China's livestream selling machine: what the hosts and their agencies say actually drives sales
**Work ID:** W7204239811 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. 'Dominant' overstates 'prominent'** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Participants identified influencer capability, influencer–agency coordination and platform strategy as the dominant success factors"
- **Abstract says:** "Prominent factors in LSIM campaign success, from LSIs' and MCN team members' perspectives, include influencer capabilities, LSI–MCN coordination and platform strategies."
- **Problem:** The abstract lists these as prominent factors among others, not as the dominant ones; 'dominant' implies a ranking the abstract does not report.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to 'as prominent success factors'."

**Issue B. Specific tension domains not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the study documents the tensions between hosts and agencies — over tools, targets and platform policy — and the workarounds both sides develop"
- **Abstract says:** "Results reveal a dynamic LSIM activity system involving interactions among LSIs, MCN team members, tools, culture and policies... shows how LSIs and MCN team members respond to activity-system contradictions through adaptive strategies."
- **Problem:** The abstract names tools, culture and policies; 'targets' (sales quotas) is not verifiable from the abstract alone.
- **Suggested fix:** "Use the abstract's own list — 'over tools, culture and platform policy' — or note that the specifics come from the full text."

### Study 16: The harsh reviewer problem: negativity reads as helpful but makes the critic look less trustworthy
**Work ID:** W7172001493 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. 'Disappeared' overstates 'mitigated'** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "The penalty disappeared when expectations were ambiguous and flipped entirely when people expected negativity"
- **Abstract says:** "the effect on credibility ... is mitigated when consumers have ambiguous prior expectations, and reverses when expectations are negative (studies 3–5)"
- **Problem:** The abstract says the effect is mitigated (reduced) under ambiguous expectations, not eliminated.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to 'The penalty was reduced when expectations were ambiguous and reversed when people expected negativity.'"

### Study 17: When your doctor is also an influencer, your skepticism switches off
**Work ID:** W7213976385 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Proposed mechanism presented as demonstrated, and extended to commercial recommendations** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the same mechanism that improves adherence to genuine medical advice also lowers consumers' guard against commercial recommendations"
- **Abstract says:** "These strategies help them maintain authority while mitigating perceptions of overt persuasion and may foster increased recommendation adherence. We propose a theory-building mechanism, the mere social media presence effect..."
- **Problem:** The abstract hedges adherence ('may foster') and frames the mechanism as proposed theory-building; it says nothing about commercial or sponsored recommendations, which the digest headline ('your skepticism switches off') and this line treat as established.
- **Suggested fix:** "Soften to 'the mechanism the authors propose may both support adherence to genuine medical advice and, they argue, mute audiences' recognition of persuasion attempts — though commercial endorsements were not directly tested.'"

### Study 18: Fast-moving brands on social media earn more word of mouth — but mainly from collectivist consumers
**Work ID:** W7213466946 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Self-presentation moderator dropped from study description** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Three online experiments tested whether consumers' perception that a brand is agile on social media — quick, responsive, adaptive — drives positive electronic word of mouth."
- **Abstract says:** "a significant three-way interaction reveals that self-presentation behaviors play a more pronounced moderating role for UK consumers"
- **Problem:** Self-presentation is a central moderator in Studies 1-2 (a three-way interaction), but it appears only glancingly in the story angles and not in the description of what was tested.
- **Suggested fix:** "Add that the model also tested self-presentation behaviors as a moderator, which mattered more for UK than Turkish participants."

**Issue B. 'Substantially stronger' firmer than abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "but the effect was substantially stronger among Turkish participants"
- **Abstract says:** "the positive impact of PSMA on e-WOM is greater for Turkish participants than for UK participants"
- **Problem:** The abstract reports a greater effect but gives no magnitude, so 'substantially' is not supported.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to 'the effect was stronger among Turkish participants'."

### Study 19: Creepy targeting doesn't just annoy people — it makes them want to blend into the crowd
**Work ID:** W7214349274 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract.

### Study 20: "The AI did it" is a risky excuse: blaming the algorithm cuts blame but signals moral indifference
**Work ID:** W7214331895 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. 'Most people' implies a proportion the study does not report** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "research suggests most people accept that the brand is less factually to blame while trusting it less as a moral actor"
- **Abstract says:** "At the factual level, this strategy increases consumers' perceived responsibility reduction... At the value level, it also triggers perceived moral indifference, thereby producing a backfire effect that damages trust."
- **Problem:** The abstract reports average condition differences, not the share of participants showing each response; 'most people' reads as a headcount finding.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to 'research suggests people on average see the brand as less factually to blame while trusting it less as a moral actor'."

### Study 21: ASMR ads land very differently for "masculine" and "feminine" brands — 15,807 YouTube comments show why
**Work ID:** W7214311277 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline implies mechanism from associational text mining** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "ASMR ads land very differently for "masculine" and "feminine" brands — 15,807 YouTube comments show why"
- **Abstract says:** "Feminine brands are associated with higher immersion scores, whereas masculine brands are associated with more sexualization-oriented discourse."
- **Problem:** The comment analysis documents a difference in discourse patterns, not the reason behind it; "show why" promises an explanatory finding the abstract does not report. The body's "drew higher immersion scores" similarly reads as an effect rather than an association.
- **Suggested fix:** "Reword to "15,807 YouTube comments show how" and use "were associated with higher immersion scores" in the body."

### Study 22: Crowdfunding titles that brag about market traction win; titles that get personal lose
**Work ID:** W7213972386 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Platform nationality not in abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Researchers analyzed 2,064 startup campaigns on the Chinese crowdfunding platform Kaishiba"
- **Abstract says:** "we examine 2,064 startups that sought funding on the Kaishiba crowdfunding platform"
- **Problem:** The abstract names the platform but never identifies it as Chinese; the descriptor (which also drives the caveat about generalizing to "Kickstarter-style Western platforms") is unverifiable from the abstract alone.
- **Suggested fix:** "Either drop "Chinese" or attribute it outside the abstract, e.g. "the Kaishiba crowdfunding platform (a China-based site)"."

**Issue B. Win/lose phrasing for correlational data** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Crowdfunding titles that brag about market traction win; titles that get personal lose"
- **Abstract says:** "market validation information in a project title is positively correlated with crowdfunding performance, whereas low psychological distance information is negatively associated with crowdfunding performance"
- **Problem:** The headline states an outcome as if causal, while the abstract reports only correlation; the digest's own caveat says causality is not established.
- **Suggested fix:** "Soften to "Crowdfunding titles that signal market traction are linked to better funding; personal, relational titles to worse"."

### Study 23: Being outnumbered changes what people buy: gender-minority settings boost appeal of gender-neutral products
**Work ID:** W7214404629 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline states behavior, study measured intention** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Being outnumbered changes what people buy: gender-minority settings boost appeal of gender-neutral products"
- **Abstract says:** "individuals in a gender-minority context show significantly higher gender alignment and purchase intentions towards gender-neutral products, with self-verification serving as a mediator"
- **Problem:** The outcome was stated purchase intention in experiments, not observed purchasing; the headline asserts a change in actual buying, which contradicts the digest's own caveat that intentions rather than purchases were measured.
- **Suggested fix:** "Change to "Being outnumbered changes what people say they'd buy" or "...shifts stated interest in gender-neutral products"."
